title: New approach to very low radiation doses needed, says nuclear industry
html:
"This confuses the public and diverts public funds, regulatory effort and industry resources to negligible risks," says World Nuclear Association. "For example, rules can be so strict that material which could be recycled must instead be managed as radioactive waste at considerable cost - with knock-on effects for energy prices, jobs and sustainability."

It notes that there is no clear scientific evidence of risk at very low doses. "Clear epidemiological evidence of health risk exists only above about 100 millisieverts (mSv)," the position statement says. "Below that level the evidence is limited and inconsistent, and at sub-mSv doses there is no clear evidence of risk at all. Any residual risk would be extremely small compared with the risks of everyday life, and lies well within the variation of natural background radiation, which averages about 3 mSv/yr worldwide and ranges up to many tens of mSv/yr."

The linear no-threshold approach assumes that risk rises in proportion to dose all the way down to zero. It was adopted as a practical basis for radiological protection and is not claimed to be a proven scientific theory. World Nuclear Association said it accepts that as the best current basis for the system, but at very low doses it is not a reliable indicator of risk or harm and "should be applied with the graded approach, not be the sole basis for decisions".

According to World Nuclear Association's Nuclear Essentials guide to radiation, eating one banana provides a dose of 0.0001 mSv, a dental X-ray 0.005 mSv, a return London to New York flight 0.08 mSv, a CT scan of the chest 6.6 mSv. It says the average yearly dose from background radon in the UK is 1.3 mSv, the yearly dose for a typical airline crew member is 3 mSv and the average yearly dose for nuclear power station workers is 0.18 mSv. Workers at nuclear power plants are warned of the risks of radiation and are carefully monitored. Yet two return trips across the Atlantic (due to cosmic rays at altitude in flight) will provide the same dose as working in the nuclear industry for a year. Neither has any measurable impact on a person's health, but they are treated very differently.

The World Nuclear Association position statement adds: "Over-conservatism leads to disproportionate and sometimes harmful outcomes. The International Commission on Radiological Protection's own guidance that societal resources should not be wasted is often ignored in practice. For example, clearance criteria can be so restrictive that actual doses are one to two orders of magnitude below the already conservative 'trivial' level of some tens of microsieverts (µSv) per year, forcing material that could be recycled to be managed as radioactive waste at considerable cost. Disproportionate controls also fuel public fear of radiation and can even increase overall harm by exposing people or the environment to greater conventional risks."

The position statement sets out five practical recommendations for the International Commission on Radiological Protection, international organisations, governments and regulators to support nuclear energy's expansion to meet the global energy challenge: adopt a simpler, graded, risk-informed approach that places greater emphasis on good governance and proportionality; give proportionality greater prominence, including in the next International Commission on Radiological Protection General Recommendations and the major publications of international organisations; pursue optimisation, not minimisation, with realistic assessments that account for all relevant risks, not radiation alone; acknowledge uncertainty in risk estimates at very low doses, so that the linear no-threshold approach is not the only input to decisions; and set a practical cut-off below which no further regulatory effort is needed.

World Nuclear Association represents more than 280 companies across the nuclear value chain around the world, and its position statement was developed in consultation with radiation protection practitioners and key international organisations. It is supported by the Association's technical report, titled Decision-Making at Very Low Doses, prepared by its Radiological Protection Working Group.

"Radiological protection has served society well, and our industry is fully committed to maintaining the highest standards," said Kari Toews, Director Occupational Safety & Senior Health Physicist at Cameco Corporation, and Chair of the Radiological Protection Working Group. "But at very low doses - levels lost within the intrinsic variation of natural background radiation - protection measures must be proportionate to the risk. Our recommendations offer a practical, evidence-based path that keeps people safe while ensuring society's resources are directed where they make a real difference, helping nuclear energy play its full part in meeting the world's growing energy needs."

Sama Bilbao y León, Director General of World Nuclear Association, said: "Nuclear energy is essential to meeting the world's growing demand for clean, reliable and affordable energy, and our industry remains fully committed to the highest standards of radiological protection. This industry position statement brings together the expertise of radiation protection specialists from across the nuclear sector to offer regulators and policymakers a practical, evidence-based way forward: maintaining robust protection while focusing effort and resources where they deliver the greatest benefit for people and the environment. Getting this right will help nuclear energy make its full contribution to meeting the global energy challenge."
summary: The current regulation of exposures to very low doses of radiation needs to be modified to end the "double standard" where doses received from things like food, the environment and airline flights are not controlled, yet those from human-made planned exposure are regulated, however small the dose, W
